en.title: Women leaders
en.summary: Women who have led countries and organisations in the English-speaking world.

paragraphs: Women have ruled and governed for centuries, but the number of women elected to lead nations is recent. This lesson presents examples and practises the structure the first woman to.

Two queens, Elizabeth I and Victoria, gave their names to ages of English history. Elected leadership came later. In 1979 Margaret Thatcher became the first woman to be prime minister of the United Kingdom. Julia Gillard held the same office in Australia from 2010 to 2013, and Jacinda Ardern, who led New Zealand from 2017 to 2023, was widely admired for her response to the Christchurch attack in 2019. In 2021 Kamala Harris took office as vice president, the first woman to do so in the United States. Despite this progress, women remain a minority among heads of government anywhere in the world.

paragraphs: **1. The first woman to + infinitive.** It is a compact way to state a record. See Introduction to Grammar: Verbs and verb phrases.

blocks.html:
PatternExample
the first woman to + verbthe first woman to lead the country
the youngest person to + verbthe youngest person to win the prize

paragraphs: **2. Despite and in spite of take a noun or -ing form.** See Introduction to Grammar: Prepositions and conjunctions.

blocks.html:
FormExample
despite + nounDespite this progress, women remain a minority.
in spite of + -ingIn spite of facing criticism, she stayed.

items: **Head of government** runs the daily business of state.
**Hold office** means to occupy a post.

paragraphs: Elected women's share in parliaments has risen steadily, but progress differs between countries. Debates about quotas and about the treatment of women in politics continue.
